nodes.label: AckDB (activity ledger and at-risk deals screen)
nodes.norm_label: ackdb (activity ledger and at-risk deals screen)
nodes.rationale: The product the benchmark is drawn from. Its demo screen reads '8 deals at risk · $1.2M' with a reason next to each deal: champion left, competitor mentioned twice, two tickets escalated, no exec calls in 30 days. On a live ledger that is thousands of small decisions a day. Its architecture diagram is labelled for a million events a day.

nodes.label: Cost to reach 100%: Jev per deal plus Claude review at half of Sonnet's cost
nodes.norm_label: cost to reach 100%: jev per deal plus claude review at half of sonnet's cost
nodes.rationale: Sonnet per deal on every deal: 100%, $0.0806, 75.1 s. Jev per deal then Claude reviewing the 9 flagged deals: 100%, $0.0399, 52.1 s. Jev per deal alone: 95%, $0.0023, 7.3 s. The hybrid costs half as much as Sonnet alone at the same accuracy because Claude never opens the 11 healthy deals. Review cost scales with the flag rate, and this set is 40% at risk, far more than a real pipeline, so the gap should be wider on real data.

nodes.label: Cost at a million events a day (AckDB design volume)
nodes.norm_label: cost at a million events a day (ackdb design volume)
nodes.rationale: Linear extrapolation from the measured per-event costs, classifying every event as it lands at the volume AckDB's architecture diagram is labelled for. Jev: $41.82 a day, $1,255 a month, about 4 calls in flight at p50. Haiku 4.5: $852.17 a day, $25,565 a month, about 28 in flight. Sonnet 5: $2,350.10 a day, $70,503 a month, about 31 in flight. Built from 73 events, so treat it as a sense of scale. Prices are published and token counts measured, so the ratio holds.

nodes.label: Review step: Claude checks Jev's flags and writes the deal-owner note
nodes.norm_label: review step: claude checks jev's flags and writes the deal-owner note
nodes.rationale: Jev cannot write text (week 01's HTTP 400), so Claude Sonnet 5 does the last step, and only on the 9 deals Jev per deal flagged. It gets the full ledger and Jev's reasons, decides whether each flag holds up, then writes the deal owner a two or three sentence Slack note naming the people, the events and one thing to do this week. With computed facts it agreed with the answer key on 9 of 9.

nodes.label: Setup claude-haiku-4-5: Haiku 4.5 per event (73 calls)
nodes.norm_label: setup claude-haiku-4-5: haiku 4.5 per event (73 calls)
nodes.rationale: One claude CLI call per event, same three questions. 8 of 8 caught, 3 false alarms (one is Oakridge, E048), 85%, 191.6 s, $0.0622, p50 2,404 ms. Severity exact 87.7%. It got the E066 Northgate trap exactly right.

nodes.label: Setup claude-sonnet-5: Sonnet 5 per event (73 calls)
nodes.norm_label: setup claude-sonnet-5: sonnet 5 per event (73 calls)
nodes.rationale: One claude CLI call per event. 8 of 8 caught, 1 false alarm (Northgate, E066 read as a serious stall), 95%, 224.3 s and $0.1716, the slowest and most expensive setup. Severity exact 87.7%.

nodes.label: Setup claude-sonnet-5-per-deal: Sonnet 5 batched per deal (20 calls)
nodes.norm_label: setup claude-sonnet-5-per-deal: sonnet 5 batched per deal (20 calls)
nodes.rationale: One claude CLI call per deal labelling every event in one answer, with spec.assess() applying the rule. The best accuracy of the week: 0 false alarms, 20 of 20, though reasons exactly right on only 6 of 8. 75.1 s, $0.0806. exec_engaged 98.6%, still missing Rachel Kim's edit to the Pinecrest order form (E046).

nodes.label: Setup jev: Jev per event (73 calls)
nodes.norm_label: setup jev: jev per event (73 calls)
nodes.rationale: One Jev request per event, three questions each. 8 of 8 caught, 1 false alarm (Oakridge, E048 read as champion_exit), 95% deal accuracy, 25.6 s for the whole ledger, $0.0031, p50 347 ms per call.

nodes.label: Setup jev-per-deal: Jev batched per deal (20 calls)
nodes.norm_label: setup jev-per-deal: jev batched per deal (20 calls)
nodes.rationale: One Jev request per deal. The whole ledger goes in as state and every event gets its own three questions keyed by event id. 8 of 8 caught, 1 false alarm (Silverline, p_exec 0.49), 95%, 7.3 s and $0.0023, the fastest and cheapest setup: 35 times cheaper and 10 times faster than Sonnet per deal at one deal less accuracy. exec_engaged 98.6%, Brier 0.009.

nodes.label: Week 02 label distribution (73 events)
nodes.rationale: signal: 32 momentum, 21 routine, 8 escalation, 5 competitor, 5 stall, 2 champion_exit. severity: 53 none, 6 watch, 13 serious, 1 critical (E033, Keystone choosing Corvid). exec_engaged: 17 true, 56 false. champion_exit has two examples, both on Vantage.

nodes.label: DEALS: synthetic ledger of 20 open deals and 73 hand-labelled events
nodes.norm_label: deals: synthetic ledger of 20 open deals and 73 hand-labelled events
nodes.rationale: The benchmark ledger, $2.79M of pipeline. Events follow the AckDB ledger format: subject first, a typed prefix on anything that is not a person doing something, raw timestamps, provider in brackets. D01 to D05 rebuild the five deals on AckDB's at-risk demo screen (Datacore, Cloudmark, Ironbridge, Precision, Vantage) so each reason has to be earned from events. The rest, and every person, are made up. Each event is (id, timestamp, source, text, signal, severity, exec_engaged) and each deal carries expect, the verdict it was written to have.

nodes.label: Per-event judgment: exec_engaged (noul, did a senior customer person take part)
nodes.norm_label: per-event judgment: exec_engaged (noul, did a senior customer person take part)
nodes.rationale: Jev noul question: did a senior customer person (VP and above, any C-level title, President or Founder) actively speak, write, decide or edit in this event? Directors, heads of department, managers and leads do not count, and neither does being cc'd, mentioned or changing jobs. The probability is cut at 0.5 and the raw p_exec is kept for the Brier score. It carries the most money because it drives no_exec_30d. Per event, Jev, Haiku and Sonnet all score 94.5%. Per deal, Jev and Sonnet both reach 98.6% (Brier 0.009 and 0.016).

nodes.label: COMPETITORS: invented competitor names (Hexline, Corvid, Tallyworks)
nodes.norm_label: competitors: invented competitor names (hexline, corvid, tallyworks)
nodes.rationale: Made up so no real product ends up in a synthetic loss report, and both models are told the names up front. Week 01 showed Jev cannot be expected to know who a company's competitors are, and week 02 is not testing that. The README credits this for the task being easier than week 01.

nodes.label: Risk reason: champion_left
nodes.rationale: A champion_exit event at serious or worse. Printed as 'champion left'. Only Vantage ($128K) has it, and both champion_exit events in the set are Vantage's, so treat results on this class as an anecdote.

nodes.label: Risk reason: closing_with_issues
nodes.rationale: The deal closes within 7 days of as_of and at least one event is serious or worse. Printed as 'closes in Nd with open issues'. Precision, closing 2026-09-28, is the only case.

nodes.label: Risk reason: competitor
nodes.rationale: Two or more competitor events at watch or worse, or one critical. Printed as 'competitor mentioned xN'. Ironbridge ($240K) and Keystone ($210K) carry it in the answer key.

nodes.label: Risk reason: escalations
nodes.rationale: Two or more escalation events at serious or worse, or one critical. Printed as 'N tickets escalated'. Cloudmark ($94K) and Precision ($62K).

nodes.label: Risk reason: no_exec_30d
nodes.rationale: The deal is worth $100K or more and no exec_engaged event falls in the 30 days before as_of. No single event can show it. It only exists across the whole ledger, which is why it lives in code. Datacore ($185K) is the answer-key case. The ledger run's six false alarms, Jev per deal's Silverline alarm and the review step's Datacore mistake all involve this rule.

nodes.label: Risk reason: stalled
nodes.rationale: A stall event at serious or worse: budget cut or frozen, seats reduced, or the deal pushed out. Printed as 'budget or timing slipped'. Halcyon ($150K) and Tidewater ($76K).

nodes.label: Per-event judgment: signal (choice of six)
nodes.rationale: Jev choice question with six options: competitor, escalation, champion_exit, stall, momentum, routine. The SIGNALS criteria are the exact strings both Jev and Claude receive, and they carry the edge cases: a competitor named only to be rejected is momentum, someone other than the champion leaving is routine, and a champion promoted inside the account is momentum. Scores: Jev 91.8% per event and 89.0% per deal, Haiku 91.8%, Sonnet 87.7% per event and 90.4% per deal.

nodes.label: Week 02: deal risk from an AckDB activity ledger
nodes.norm_label: week 02: deal risk from an ackdb activity ledger
nodes.rationale: 20 open deals, 73 events in AckDB's ledger format, three typed judgments per event, a rule in code that turns them into reasons, and Claude writing the note to the deal owner at the end. Jev (TypeSafe AI) against Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 in six setups. How the work is split turned out to matter as much as the model.

nodes.label: results.json (week 02 scored output, six setups)
nodes.rationale: Written by score.py from results/raw/*.jsonl. All six runs scored all 20 deals with no failures, caught 8 of 8 at-risk deals and missed $0 of ARR. They differ on false alarms (jev 1, jev-per-deal 1, claude-haiku-4-5 3, claude-sonnet-5 1, claude-sonnet-5-per-deal 0, claude-sonnet-5-ledger 6), cost and time. Event-level scores exist for every run except the ledger run, which returns a verdict instead of labels.

nodes.label: Week 02 rubric: how the deal-risk answer key was written
nodes.norm_label: week 02 rubric: how the deal-risk answer key was written
nodes.rationale: 73 events across 20 open deals, every label by hand, against the same strings the models get, so disagreeing with a label means disagreeing with a visible rule that can be changed in src/ledger.py. Today is fixed at 2026-09-25 for the two rules that count days.

nodes.label: House rule: keep arithmetic out of prompts
nodes.norm_label: house rule: keep arithmetic out of prompts
nodes.rationale: Thresholds, date windows and counts go in code. Week 02 measured the alternative: the same model scored 100% when code applied the rule and 70% when it applied the rule itself.

nodes.label: Hand the agent day counts instead of date arithmetic
nodes.norm_label: hand the agent day counts instead of date arithmetic
nodes.rationale: In week 02, Claude reviewing Jev's flags decided an August 15 meeting fell inside a 30 day window ending September 25, while getting everything else right. An agent that reviews what these tools return should be given the numbers and never asked to count days.

nodes.label: Week 02 rule thresholds ($100K exec rule, 30 days, 7 days to close)
nodes.norm_label: week 02 rule thresholds ($100k exec rule, 30 days, 7 days to close)
nodes.rationale: The tools apply the week 02 rule as written. The thresholds suit the synthetic pipeline in the repo and a real pipeline will want its own. The README points to the top of week-02-deal-risk/src/spec.py, but the numbers are inline in assess() and repeated in the RISK_RULES text.

nodes.label: Batch by deal (per-entity batching)
nodes.rationale: Design rule 1. If a judgment depends on who someone is, and that is established elsewhere in the ledger, per-event classification has a ceiling. Sending the whole deal in one request fixes the shared misses and cuts round trips from 73 to 20.

nodes.label: Check the category before the magnitude
nodes.norm_label: check the category before the magnitude
nodes.rationale: spec.assess() looks at the signal before the severity, so an over-rated routine event, such as a page visit rated watch, cannot raise an alarm. That is why Jev's severity bias cost it no false alarms. Put the category check before the magnitude check in your own rules and the bias matters much less.

nodes.label: Finding: Sonnet applying the risk rule itself scored 70%, 100% when code applied it
nodes.norm_label: finding: sonnet applying the risk rule itself scored 70%, 100% when code applied it
nodes.rationale: Same model, same ledger. Sonnet labelling events with spec.assess() applying the rule got 20 of 20. Sonnet reading the ledger and applying RISK_RULES itself got 14 of 20. All six false alarms were no_exec_30d, the one rule with a threshold and date arithmetic: three deals under $100K (Marlow, Oakridge, Fairhaven) and three with an exec engaged 12, 17 and 29 days before today. Counting two at-risk deals where it added the reason anyway, it got no_exec_30d wrong on 8 of 20. This is week 01's routing-belongs-in-code point with a number on it.

nodes.label: Review step's date-arithmetic error on Datacore, fixed by passing computed facts
nodes.norm_label: review step's date-arithmetic error on datacore, fixed by passing computed facts
nodes.rationale: The first review version got 8 of 9. It correctly threw out Silverline, then also threw out Datacore, which really is at risk, saying the CTO's August 15 engagement was inside the 30-day window. August 15 is 41 days before September 25. It fixed a false alarm by creating a missed $185K deal, the worse of the two errors. brief.py --facts now passes the arithmetic from code: whether the deal clears $100K, days to close, and when Jev last saw a senior person take part. Claude can still overrule judgment calls and did so correctly on Silverline, but no longer does the subtraction. 9 of 9.

nodes.label: Jev does not check who left (E048 Oakridge false alarm)
nodes.norm_label: jev does not check who left (e048 oakridge false alarm)
nodes.rationale: E048 is a support agent leaving Oakridge, and the deal record names a different champion. Jev per event called it champion_exit, serious, and raised a false alarm. So did Haiku. Sonnet compared the name with the record and called it routine both times. Checking a fact against the record is Claude's strength, same as week 01.

nodes.label: The trap that caught Sonnet (E066 Northgate CCO urgency)
nodes.norm_label: the trap that caught sonnet (e066 northgate cco urgency)
nodes.rationale: E066 is the Northgate Chief Customer Officer: 'I need this live by November 15 or we have a problem. What do you need from us to get there?' She is pushing to buy faster, so the label is momentum, severity none. rubric.md predicted models would get it wrong. Haiku got it exactly right. Sonnet per event called it a serious stall and raised a false alarm on a healthy $160K deal. Jev got the signal right and still rated it serious, which is its severity bias again.

nodes.label: Jev's upward severity bias (score questions run about half a level high)
nodes.norm_label: jev's upward severity bias (score questions run about half a level high)
nodes.rationale: Jev's exact severity is 63 to 67% against Claude's 88%, and the misses lean one way: 21 of 24 per event and 24 of 27 per deal rate the event as more threatening than it is. Second week running: week 01's intent scores ran high in the same way, and both are score questions. Expect about half a level of upward bias from Jev's score type and correct for it. It cost no false alarms here because spec.assess checks the signal before the severity.

nodes.label: Keep arithmetic out of prompts
nodes.rationale: Design rule 2. Thresholds, date windows and counts belong in code. Every model error in the benchmark that involved a number was a model doing maths it should have been given, as in the ledger run's no_exec_30d alarms and the review step's Datacore date.

nodes.label: Finding: Jev, Haiku and Sonnet miss the same four events per event (exec title only in an earlier event)
nodes.norm_label: finding: jev, haiku and sonnet miss the same four events per event (exec title only in an earlier event)
nodes.rationale: Judged one event at a time, Jev, Haiku and Sonnet all score exactly 94.5% on exec_engaged and all miss E026, E033, E046 and E055. Each is a message from an exec whose title only appears in an earlier event: E026 is from Grace Liu, known to be the CFO only from the E025 meeting. A better model cannot fix it because the title is not in the event. Given the whole deal, Jev per deal gets all four and Sonnet per deal gets three. rubric.md flagged this as a structural trap before the runs, and the README calls it the sturdiest finding of the week.

nodes.label: Silverline p_exec 0.49: a coin flip that became a false alarm
nodes.norm_label: silverline p_exec 0.49: a coin flip that became a false alarm
nodes.rationale: Jev per deal's one false alarm. Silverline is the biggest deal in the set at $300K. The E068 SVP sponsor call, 29 days before today, scored p_exec 0.49, one hundredth under the line, so the deal was flagged for no exec engagement. A hard 0.5 cutoff turned an honest 'I don't know' into an alarm. Route anything between 0.4 and 0.6 to a person and treat Jev's probabilities as a band (design rule 3). The review step correctly threw this flag out by pointing at the SVP call.

nodes.label: What I would ship: Jev per deal, spec.assess in code, Claude on flagged deals only
nodes.norm_label: what i would ship: jev per deal, spec.assess in code, claude on flagged deals only
nodes.rationale: Event lands in AckDB, Jev answers three typed questions batched per deal, spec.assess() applies every threshold and date in code, and only flagged deals go to Claude, which checks the flag against the ledger with the arithmetic handed to it and then writes the note. Three rules: batch by deal, keep arithmetic out of prompts, treat Jev's probabilities as a band. The MCP server wraps this pipeline as a tool so an agent can run the sweep without reading the ledger.

nodes.label: exec_engaged 30-day window test events (E004 Datacore, E051 Summit Labs, E068 Silverline)
nodes.norm_label: exec_engaged 30-day window test events (e004 datacore, e051 summit labs, e068 silverline)
nodes.rationale: Three events built around no_exec_30d. E004: Datacore's CTO is only cc'd, so the last real exec contact is the meeting 41 days earlier and the $185K deal is at risk. E051: a Summit Labs VP is cc'd but ran a meeting twelve days before, so the deal is fine. E068: the Silverline SVP sponsor call was 29 days before today, one day inside the window, on the biggest deal in the set.

nodes.label: Signal edge-case traps (E036, E048, E044, E031, E073, E072)
nodes.norm_label: signal edge-case traps (e036, e048, e044, e031, e073, e072)
nodes.rationale: The traps sit on the edges between signals. A competitor named to be rejected (E036, Lumen Health) is momentum. Someone other than the champion leaving (E048, a support agent at Oakridge) is routine, because the champion is named on the deal record. A champion promoted inside the account (E044, Pinecrest) is momentum. How-to tickets (E031, E073) are routine. Layoffs where the team says the renewal is protected (E072, Driftwood) are stall at watch.

nodes.label: jev-gtm MCPServer and its agent instructions
nodes.norm_label: jev-gtm mcpserver and its agent instructions
nodes.rationale: The server is named jev-gtm and runs over stdio. Its instructions tell the agent the tools return labels and probabilities and never prose, so the agent writes any email or summary itself, and say which tool fits which job: triage_lead for a new inbound lead, deal_risk for one deal's activity, deals_at_risk to sweep a whole ledger export without reading it.

nodes.label: LEDGER_DIR (JEV_LEDGER_DIR root for ledger exports)
nodes.rationale: Resolved from the JEV_LEDGER_DIR environment variable and defaults to week-02-deal-risk/data. It is the only folder deals_at_risk may open a file from.

nodes.label: mcp.example.json
nodes.rationale: Config to copy for clients that take JSON, such as Claude Desktop. Registers the jev-gtm server as `uv run --quiet .../mcp-server/jev_server.py` with TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_LEDGER_DIR in its env.

nodes.label: TYPESAFE_API_KEY (kept in gitignored .env.local)
nodes.rationale: Lives in .env.local, which is gitignored and has never been committed. .env.example documents the shape.

nodes.label: CRM MCP server
nodes.rationale: Where inbound form fills land, and where the agent sets owner and stage from the route triage_lead returns.

nodes.label: Enrichment MCP server (headcount, titles, funding)
nodes.rationale: Runs before triage_lead in the inbound flow. Its headcount should be passed through, because segment reads headcount directly and a lead that arrives with headcount gets segmented from a number instead of a guess.

nodes.label: Inbound lead workflow (enrichment, triage_lead, CRM, Slack)
nodes.norm_label: inbound lead workflow (enrichment, triage_lead, crm, slack)
nodes.rationale: A form fill lands in the CRM, the enrichment server adds headcount, title and company type, triage_lead returns disqualify, icp_fit, segment, intent and a route, the CRM server sets owner and stage from the route, and only ae_now or sdr_sequence leads get an agent-written first email drafted in Slack. Enrichment goes first because segment reads headcount directly. In week 01, 29 of 60 leads earned an email and the other 31 cost about four thousandths of a cent each to reject or nurture.

nodes.label: MCP SDK 2.x move (FastMCP became MCPServer)
nodes.rationale: In mcp 2.x FastMCP became MCPServer in mcp.server.mcpserver, and results use structured_content and is_error where 1.x used camelCase. The server pins mcp>=2.2,<3.

nodes.label: Monday risk sweep workflow (activity database, deals_at_risk, Slack)
nodes.norm_label: monday risk sweep workflow (activity database, deals_at_risk, slack)
nodes.rationale: The activity database exports the week's ledger to JEV_LEDGER_DIR, deals_at_risk checks every deal and returns only the risky ones, the agent checks each flag against the ledger and writes a note to each owner, and the Slack server posts them. Given a plain request, Claude Code called deals_at_risk once and returned all eight at-risk deals from the week 02 answer key ($1.145M, correct reasons), then added that Precision is the smallest deal and the most urgent because it closes in three days. Jev made 219 small decisions and the agent never opened the ledger.

nodes.label: Slack MCP server
nodes.rationale: Where the agent drafts first emails for reps in the inbound flow and posts owner notes after the Monday risk sweep.

nodes.label: uv run with inline script dependencies
nodes.norm_label: uv run with inline script dependencies
nodes.rationale: jev_server.py and check.py declare `mcp>=2.2,<3` in a `# /// script` header, so `uv run` fetches the MCP SDK on first run and there is nothing to install. The benchmarks themselves use only the Python standard library.

nodes.label: Working in this repo (CLAUDE.md)
nodes.rationale: Repo instructions for agents: query the graph first, follow the house rules, re-run a week's benchmark after changing a prompt the MCP server loads, write plainly, and keep the API key out of git.

nodes.label: Using this from an agent (MCP server README)
nodes.norm_label: using this from an agent (mcp server readme)
nodes.rationale: Each week ends with a working pipeline, and this folder puts those pipelines behind an MCP server so an agent that already talks to GTM tools can hand Jev the decisions. Deciding is where the bill goes: every row the agent looks at costs frontier model tokens, and most of those decisions are the typed kind Jev does at a fraction of the price and a tenth of the latency.

nodes.label: Jev Playground (weekly benchmark repo)
nodes.rationale: Every week the author builds something real with Jev and publishes the numbers. Week 01, lead triage: Jev routed 90% of leads correctly at 366 ms and $0.04 per thousand against Sonnet 5's 78% at 2.6 s and $3.01. Week 02, deal risk from an AckDB activity ledger: every setup caught all 8 at-risk deals, and Jev did the whole ledger in 7.3 s for $0.0023 with one false alarm.

nodes.label: Query the graphify graph before reading files
nodes.norm_label: query the graphify graph before reading files
nodes.rationale: graphify-out/ holds a knowledge graph so an agent does not burn a context window rediscovering how the benchmark fits together. Answers come back with file:line, and `graphify update` refreshes the graph after code changes.

nodes.label: Do the fan-out inside the tool
nodes.norm_label: do the fan-out inside the tool
nodes.rationale: Letting the agent read the ledger and call deal_risk once per deal works, but every event passes through the agent's context on the way in. On the week 02 ledger the file is 20,042 bytes and what deals_at_risk hands back is 669 bytes, for 20 deals. The ledger grows with events and the answer only with deals at risk. So the tool reads the file itself, fans out to Jev on eight threads, applies the rule in code, and returns only what someone should act on.

nodes.label: JEV_LEDGER_DIR path restriction on deals_at_risk
nodes.rationale: deals_at_risk resolves the requested name under LEDGER_DIR and refuses anything that is not a file inside it, including ../../.env.local, where the API key lives. check.py asks for that path and exits unless the call comes back as an error.

nodes.label: Tool description fix (agent searched the filesystem)
nodes.norm_label: tool description fix (agent searched the filesystem)
nodes.rationale: The first deals_at_risk description said the file lived inside the directory set by JEV_LEDGER_DIR. Claude took that as an instruction to find it and made four shell calls first, one a `find /` across the whole disk. The description now says to pass just the file name and that the server opens it, which took the run from 7 turns to 4 and cut searching to a single `ls`. The description is the only instruction an agent gets about a tool.

nodes.label: ToolError for expected failures instead of ValueError
nodes.norm_label: toolerror for expected failures instead of valueerror
nodes.rationale: Raising ValueError from the path check made the SDK log a traceback and send the agent a blank failure it could not learn from. ToolError from mcp.server.mcpserver.exceptions is for failures you saw coming: the agent gets the message and can fix its call.

nodes.label: TypedDict returns for structured tool output
nodes.norm_label: typeddict returns for structured tool output
nodes.rationale: The SDK decides whether a tool has structured output from its return annotation, and `-> dict` does not count. Results still arrived as JSON text, which hid the problem. Each tool now returns a TypedDict (Lead, DealRisk, Sweep), so it has an output schema and clients get structured content. check.py exits if structured content is missing, because the first version quietly fell back to parsing text.

nodes.label: Decisions vs writing split
nodes.rationale: Whether Jev beats Claude is the boring question. The useful one is which steps of a real workflow are decisions and which are writing, and what happens to latency and cost when a frontier model stops doing the decisions. Week 01 gives the judgments to Jev and the email to Sonnet, and the MCP tools return labels and leave the writing to the agent.

nodes.label: Setup claude-sonnet-5-ledger: Sonnet 5 reads the whole ledger and applies the rule itself (20 calls)
nodes.norm_label: setup claude-sonnet-5-ledger: sonnet 5 reads the whole ledger and applies the rule itself (20 calls)
nodes.rationale: One call per deal that reads the whole ledger and returns an at_risk probability and reason keys under RISK_RULES. This is how most people would use Claude for the job, so it gets its own run. 8 of 8 caught but 6 false alarms, 70%, reasons exactly right on 6 of 8, 67.5 s, $0.0566. No event labels, so no event-level scores.

nodes.label: RISK_RULES: the deal risk rule written in words
nodes.norm_label: risk_rules: the deal risk rule written in words
nodes.rationale: The same six-reason rule as spec.assess(), written in words with the bracketed reason keys, the $100K threshold and the 30-day window. The claude-sonnet-5-ledger setup and the brief.py review prompt get this text and have to apply it themselves. Every other setup hands its event labels to spec.assess().

nodes.label: Per-event judgment: severity (score over none, watch, serious, critical)
nodes.norm_label: per-event judgment: severity (score over none, watch, serious, critical)
nodes.rationale: Jev score question over four ordered levels. Each event is judged on its own with the deal record as context, and good news is always none. jev.read() rounds Jev's continuous score to the nearest level. Exact match: Jev 67.1% per event and 63.0% per deal, every Claude setup 87.7%. Within one level every setup is 97.3% or better.

nodes.label: Label-leak guard: the answer lives next to the deal, never inside it
nodes.norm_label: label-leak guard: the answer lives next to the deal, never inside it
nodes.rationale: bench.run() asserts that 'label' is not a key of the deal dict and sends models only visible() event fields (id, ts, source, text). ledger.rows() splits the hand labels off each event first. Everything in deal and seen goes to a model, so the answer has to sit beside them.

nodes.label: Claude CLI fairness corrections (thinking off, CLI overhead subtracted, cache-rate billing)
nodes.norm_label: claude cli fairness corrections (thinking off, cli overhead subtracted, cache-rate billing)
nodes.rationale: The same three corrections as week 01, since the claude CLI has not changed. call() turns thinking off (MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0, --effort low) and strips the dynamic system prompt and all tools. calibrate() takes the median of five empty calls as the CLI's own scaffolding (2,822 tokens for Haiku and 3,823 for Sonnet this week) and cost() subtracts it. cost() bills cache writes at 1.25x and cache reads at 0.1x the input rate.

nodes.label: COMPETITOR_CLARIFICATION (v2 prompt delta)
nodes.rationale: Round 1 said 'a direct competitor' and never said who that is, so Haiku threw out Workday, Atlassian, ServiceNow and Oracle for also selling software. That is a fair complaint about the prompt, not only the model, so round 2 names Clay, Apollo, ZoomInfo, Outreach and Salesloft and changes nothing else. Both models get it.

nodes.label: LEADS (60 hand-labelled lead records)
nodes.rationale: Each tuple carries the lead fields and the four hand-written labels (disqualify, icp_fit, segment, intent). No model produced any label, and no route is stored: spec.route() computes it from the labels so the answer key and the models go through the same function. main() splits each record into a lead payload and a labels payload in data/leads.jsonl.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: disqualify (noul / probability)
nodes.rationale: Asked as a noul (probability) question so the answer carries calibration, not just a boolean. Explicitly tells the model not to disqualify a real buyer for a personal email address, a short message, or a small company.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: icp_fit (noul / probability)
nodes.rationale: Three conjunctive conditions (B2B, 50+ employees, revenue/marketing/ops/data/exec role), judged on company and role rather than email domain, and deliberately kept independent of disqualify.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: intent (score over an ordered ladder)
nodes.norm_label: typed judgment: intent (score over an ordered ladder)
nodes.rationale: Modelled as a continuous score over four ordered levels rather than a choice, judging urgency and specificity of the message and not company quality. This is the one judgment where Jev loses to both Claude models.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: segment (choice)
nodes.rationale: A choice question over enterprise / mid_market / smb driven by headcount, with inference from the company name only when headcount is missing. Every runner scores 95-100% on it, which is what makes it useful as a floor.

nodes.label: v1 / v2 prompt variants
nodes.rationale: v1 is the prompt as originally written; v2 is v1 plus one sentence naming the competitor set on the disqualify question and nothing else, so the round-to-round delta is attributable to exactly that sentence. Unknown variant strings raise rather than silently falling back to v1.

nodes.label: Six-step inbound lead triage workflow
nodes.rationale: Steps 1 to 4 (disqualify, icp_fit, segment, intent) are judgments and go to a model. Step 5, the queue, is a rule and runs in code for every runner. Step 6, the first email, is writing and goes to Claude because Jev cannot write.

nodes.label: Rubric: icp_fit rule
nodes.rationale: True when the company sells to businesses, has 50 or more people, and the role touches revenue, marketing, operations or data or is an executive. Judge the company and not the email domain (L016, a Cisco buyer on gmail), and look at what the role does (L044, a Facilities Coordinator at Salesforce, is no fit).

nodes.label: Rubric: intent rule
nodes.rationale: Four ordered levels (none, researching, evaluating, ready_to_buy) read from the message itself and never from company quality. Support tickets from large existing customers (L046, L048) are none. An existing customer adding 20 seats (L047) is ready_to_buy, because expansion is a purchase.

nodes.label: 60-lead label distribution
nodes.rationale: 12 disqualify and 48 not; 44 icp_fit and 16 not; 24 enterprise, 19 mid_market, 17 smb; intent 13 none, 14 researching, 20 evaluating, 13 ready_to_buy; routes 16 ae_now, 19 nurture, 10 sdr_sequence, 12 reject, 3 self_serve. self_serve has only 3 cases, so treat that row as directional.

nodes.label: Rubric: segment rule
nodes.rationale: Straight from headcount: 1000 or more is enterprise, 200 to 999 mid_market, under 200 smb. It is the easiest question and is in the set on purpose as a floor: getting it wrong means the model did not read the record.

nodes.label: Week 01: inbound lead triage and routing
nodes.norm_label: week 01: inbound lead triage and routing
nodes.rationale: 60 hand-labelled leads. Jev routed 90.0% correctly against Sonnet 5's 78.3% and Haiku 4.5's 53.3%, at 366 ms p50 and $0.042 per 1,000 leads against Sonnet's 2,571 ms and $3.006. Jev binned 0 of 16 funded buyers where Haiku binned 7, and ran about 7 times faster and 70 times cheaper than the closest Claude model on quality.

nodes.label: Lead triage rubric and answer key
nodes.norm_label: lead triage rubric and answer key
nodes.rationale: Every label in data/leads.jsonl was written by hand against these rules and no model produced any label. If Claude had written the key, scoring Claude against it would measure self-agreement and Jev would lose a point everywhere Claude was wrong. The rules are published so readers can disagree, and the fix for a mislabelled lead is a pull request against src/build_dataset.py.

nodes.label: Tools load their questions from each week's spec.py
nodes.norm_label: tools load their questions from each week's spec.py
nodes.rationale: Change a prompt in a week's spec.py and the tool changes with it, so a benchmark number in the repo describes what the tool does, as long as the benchmark is re-run after the change. load() imports each spec.py by file path under its own name, because both weeks call the module spec.py and a plain import would return whichever loaded first.

nodes.label: House rule: the answer key is written by hand
nodes.norm_label: house rule: the answer key is written by hand
nodes.rationale: If a model writes the labels, scoring that model against them measures self-agreement and quietly penalises every other model for disagreeing. Every label is hand-written against a published rubric you can argue with.

nodes.label: House rule: both sides get the same words
nodes.norm_label: house rule: both sides get the same words
nodes.rationale: The prompts are generated from one shared spec file. Jev gets the criteria as typed questions and Claude gets the same strings rendered as text, so nobody gets a hint the other did not get.

nodes.label: Sequential runs preserve latency validity
nodes.rationale: Running the calls concurrently would finish sooner and make every latency number meaningless, because they would all be queued behind each other.

nodes.label: Deliberately awkward lead set
nodes.rationale: Roughly a third of the leads are awkward on purpose: real buyers on personal email, competitors posing as buyers, huge companies with no fit, senior people with no intent, and two nearly empty messages. A set of obvious cases puts every model at 100% and tells you nothing.

nodes.label: Judgment independence (icp_fit judged separately from disqualify)
nodes.norm_label: judgment independence (icp_fit judged separately from disqualify)
nodes.rationale: A RevOps manager at a competitor is a fit on company and role and still gets rejected, because the routing rule checks disqualification first. Keeping the questions separate stops one judgment from quietly absorbing another, and a model that confuses the two shows up in the numbers.

nodes.label: PRICING and cache multipliers
nodes.rationale: List prices for Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5, with cache writes at 1.25x and cache reads at 0.1x the base input rate. The CLI caches the system prompt, a saving a production deployment would also get, so Claude gets credit for it instead of paying list price on every cached token.

nodes.label: Split-call ablation (one Claude call per question)
nodes.norm_label: split-call ablation (one claude call per question)
nodes.rationale: Run to answer the objection that asking four questions at once strawmanned Claude. Haiku's 29 icp_fit errors all ran the same direction and lined up with 27 over-disqualifications. Four calls per lead lifted icp_fit from 51.7% to 71.7% and route accuracy from 53.3% to 61.7% and nearly halved the Brier score, at 5.2 times the latency and 2.9 times the cost, and still lost to Jev by 28 points.

nodes.label: Result record: claude-haiku-4-5-split
nodes.rationale: The v1-split ablation: 61.7% route accuracy and icp_fit up to 71.7% with Brier nearly halved, at 13,631ms p50 and $3.933 per 1,000 across 4 calls per lead.

nodes.label: Result record: claude-sonnet-5
nodes.rationale: v1: 78.3% route accuracy, 2,571ms p50, $3.006 per 1,000, 1 of 16 buyers binned. v2 improves to 80.0% route accuracy, disqualify 90.0%, 0 buyers binned and 0 leaked, and cost falls to $2.22.

nodes.label: House rule: fix the unfair thing even when it helps the other side
nodes.norm_label: house rule: fix the unfair thing even when it helps the other side
nodes.rationale: Week 01 started with Claude burning 1,800 thinking tokens and 22 seconds per lead because the CLI turns thinking on by default, and turning it off took Claude to 2.6 s. Prompt caching was billed at full price until caught. claude_runner.py applies every Claude-favouring correction because a benchmark that only corrects in one direction is not worth publishing, and CLAUDE.md asks for each fix to be written down.

nodes.label: Correlated-error hypothesis (Haiku conflates disqualify and icp_fit)
nodes.norm_label: correlated-error hypothesis (haiku conflates disqualify and icp_fit)
nodes.rationale: All 29 of Haiku's icp_fit errors ran the same direction and lined up with 27 over-disqualifications: it decided 'bad lead' once and wrote that answer into both fields. That could be an artifact of the single-JSON format rather than the model, so the ablation removes the format to test it.

nodes.label: Emails written only for ae_now and sdr_sequence leads
nodes.norm_label: emails written only for ae_now and sdr_sequence leads
nodes.rationale: Gating the expensive writing step on the cheap triage step is where the end-to-end saving comes from: 29 of 60 leads earned an email and the other 31 cost nothing to write to.

nodes.label: Claude through the CLI instead of the API (duration_api_ms, scaffolding subtracted)
nodes.norm_label: claude through the cli instead of the api (duration_api_ms, scaffolding subtracted)
nodes.rationale: There was no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY on the benchmark machine, so Claude ran through the claude CLI. Latency is duration_api_ms, which excludes process startup, and token counts have the measured CLI scaffolding subtracted. Both choices favour Claude, and wiring in an API key should move the numbers slightly further in Claude's favour.

nodes.label: Fairness correction: CLI token-overhead calibration
nodes.rationale: Because of the caching, the calibration probe read the wrong field and measured Sonnet's CLI scaffolding as 2 tokens instead of 2,214, so Claude was billed for a prompt it did not write. Fixing it dropped Sonnet's cost per thousand from $7.71 to $3.01.

nodes.label: Do not read the partial run
nodes.norm_label: do not read the partial run
nodes.rationale: At 18 leads the split run sat at 88.9% and looked like it had closed the gap. At 60 leads it was 61.7%.

nodes.label: Fairness correction: prompt-cache-aware pricing
nodes.rationale: Sonnet's CLI caches the system prompt, so its real token count lands in cache_creation and cache_read instead of input_tokens. Cache reads were being charged at full input price. Cache writes bill at 1.25x and reads at 0.1x, and Claude now gets credit for that.

nodes.label: Fairness correction: extended thinking disabled
nodes.rationale: The Claude CLI enables extended thinking by default. Haiku spent about 1,800 thinking tokens and 22 seconds per lead working out whether a resume was a resume. MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 took the same call to 2.6 seconds. Nobody would ship lead triage with thinking on, so benchmarking it that way would have been dishonest by a factor of 23.

nodes.label: USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN ($42 per billion, input only)
nodes.rationale: Output tokens are not billed at all, because the output is a label and a number rather than prose.

nodes.label: Per-call cost, Jev against Sonnet 5
nodes.rationale: One lead through triage_lead costs $0.00004 on Jev against $0.0030 for the same work on Sonnet 5. One deal through deal_risk costs $0.00012 against $0.0040. A million ledger events a day runs about $1,255 a month against about $70,500. The agent's own tokens come on top, and the fan-out rule keeps those small.

nodes.label: Jev typed decision model
nodes.rationale: Send it state and typed questions and it returns a choice, a score, or a probability with a confidence attached. There is no text output. Input bills at $42 per billion tokens and output is free, since the output is a label and a number.

nodes.label: noul probability with a 0.5 decision threshold
nodes.norm_label: noul probability with a 0.5 decision threshold
nodes.rationale: A noul answer is a probability, not a boolean: 0.5 is applied as the decision threshold for the prediction while the raw probability is kept separately so calibration (Brier, ECE) can be scored without re-running the benchmark.

nodes.label: Business error metric: funded buyers binned
nodes.norm_label: business error metric: funded buyers binned
nodes.rationale: Counts leads whose true route is ae_now but whose predicted route is reject. Accuracy treats every mistake the same; this one does not, because binning a funded buyer costs revenue. Haiku did it to 7 of 16, Sonnet to 1, Jev to 0.

nodes.label: Business error metric: disqualified leads leaked
nodes.norm_label: business error metric: disqualified leads leaked
nodes.rationale: Counts leads labelled disqualify that the model let through. Handing a competitor a demo costs something worse than revenue; this is where Jev's 2-of-12 competitor blind spot shows up against the 90% headline.

nodes.label: Route accuracy (the end-to-end workflow metric)
nodes.rationale: How often the whole workflow put the lead in the right queue, which is the only number a GTM team feels. Computed by pushing both the prediction and the label through the same spec.route().

nodes.label: End-to-end cost per 1,000 inbound leads
nodes.rationale: Jev triage with Sonnet writing costs $1.31 per 1,000 leads against $4.28 for Sonnet doing both, 3.3x cheaper end to end. The saving grows the worse the inbound is, because junk never reaches the expensive step.

nodes.label: Rubric: disqualify rule
nodes.rationale: True for job applicants, students or academics asking for free access, vendors and agencies selling to us, employees of a direct competitor, and generic spam. False for everyone else, including weak and early buyers, short messages and gmail addresses. Competitors are judged by where they work: L009 and L010 read like ordinary demo requests.

nodes.label: Rubric: five-branch routing rule
nodes.rationale: Routing is a rule, so it runs as one. spec.route() takes the four judgments and returns reject, ae_now, sdr_sequence, self_serve or nurture, runs over the answer key and every model's output alike, and no model is ever asked to route. Five branches are free, instant and testable, and a model call there buys nothing and adds a way to fail.

nodes.label: Result record: jev
nodes.rationale: v1: 90.0% route accuracy, 366ms p50, $0.042 per 1,000, Brier 0.041/0.041, 0 of 16 funded buyers binned, 2 of 12 disqualified leaked. v2 holds route accuracy at exactly 90.0% with icp_fit up to 96.7%.

nodes.label: Competitor list in the prompt (Hexline, Corvid, Tallyworks)
nodes.norm_label: competitor list in the prompt (hexline, corvid, tallyworks)
nodes.rationale: The competitor names in the week 02 prompt are made up and should be replaced with real ones, because week 01 showed Jev will not work out who a company's competitors are on its own.

nodes.label: Routing belongs in code, not a model
nodes.norm_label: routing belongs in code, not a model
nodes.rationale: Five branches that are free, instant, testable and cannot drift. Spending a model call on a branch buys nothing and adds a failure mode you paid for. What the models are for is the four genuinely fuzzy judgments underneath.

nodes.label: Jev's competitor blind spot (L009 Clay, L010 Apollo.io)
nodes.norm_label: jev's competitor blind spot (l009 clay, l010 apollo.io)
nodes.rationale: Jev's two disqualify misses were a RevOps manager at Clay and a PM at Apollo.io, waved through at 0.06 and 0.18. Naming the competitor set in round 2 flipped both for Sonnet (0.95 and 0.97) and moved Jev only to 0.27 and 0.23: Jev applies the rubric it is given and does not know who the companies are. A competitor check is a domain lookup against a list the CRO already keeps, so it belongs in code.

nodes.label: Jev's half-level intent optimism bias
nodes.rationale: Intent is Jev's worst number at 75% against Sonnet's 82%. Of 15 errors, 14 are off by exactly one level and all run the same way: it reads leads as keener than they are. The bias is consistent enough that a threshold shift fixes it, and until then the intent score should go to a human review queue.

nodes.label: Recommended production architecture (blocklist, Jev, route in code, Sonnet writes)
nodes.norm_label: recommended production architecture (blocklist, jev, route in code, sonnet writes)
nodes.rationale: A domain blocklist goes first because it is the one step with a right answer that needs no model. Jev takes the four fuzzy judgments at 366 ms and $0.042 per 1,000. Routing stays in code: five branches, free, instant and unit-testable. Only qualified leads reach Sonnet. Jev's Brier score of 0.041 against Sonnet's 0.130 means its probabilities can drive the flow: send everything over 0.9 straight through and queue the 0.4 to 0.6 band for a human.

nodes.label: SYSTEM email-writing prompt
nodes.rationale: Conditions the email on the triage judgments already made, so an enterprise ready_to_buy lead gets a different email from a mid-market evaluating one. Bans generic openers, exclamation marks and em dashes; 10 of 29 outputs contained an em dash anyway.

nodes.label: Warm connection latency (979 ms first call, 360 ms median)
nodes.norm_label: warm connection latency (979 ms first call, 360 ms median)
nodes.rationale: The first call on a fresh connection pays for the TLS handshake. Eight triage_lead calls in a row through the server took 979 ms for the first and a median of 360 ms for the rest. ask() keeps one warm HTTPS connection per thread.

nodes.label: Email quirks: em dashes and a CLI signature leak
nodes.norm_label: email quirks: em dashes and a cli signature leak
nodes.rationale: The prompt says no em dashes and 10 of the 29 emails have one anyway, so house style needs post-processing. The emails are signed with a name that was never in the prompt, so the CLI is leaking something from the environment. Neither affects the triage numbers.

nodes.label: Step 6: write the first-touch email
nodes.rationale: Jev has three question types (choice, score, noul) and no text type, and asking for one returns HTTP 400, so Sonnet writes the emails conditioned on Jev's judgments. 29 of 60 leads earned one at a mean of 4,052 ms and $0.0026 each. One of them went to L009, the Clay competitor Jev let through.

nodes.label: results.json (scored benchmark output)
nodes.rationale: Seven scored records: jev, claude-haiku-4-5 and claude-sonnet-5 at v1 and v2, plus the v1-split Haiku ablation. All seven report 60 completed leads and 0 failed calls.

nodes.label: Result record: claude-haiku-4-5
nodes.rationale: v1: 53.3% route accuracy, 2,630ms p50, $1.339 per 1,000, 7 of 16 funded buyers binned, Brier 0.365/0.383. Naming the competitors in v2 made it worse on routing (51.7%) and binned 9 of 16 buyers.

nodes.label: House rule: README numbers come from a committed run in results/raw/
nodes.norm_label: house rule: readme numbers come from a committed run in results/raw/
nodes.rationale: Never hand-edit a results table. If a number changes, re-run and re-score.

nodes.label: Writing rules (plain English, no em dashes)
nodes.norm_label: writing rules (plain english, no em dashes)
nodes.rationale: Plain English the way an engineer writes notes for another engineer: no em dashes, no 'it is not X, it is Y', no stock marketing words, no section that only restates the one above. Say the number, say what it means, move on.

nodes.label: House rules for the benchmarks
nodes.rationale: The rules the author holds the benchmarks to, and the reason the numbers come out lower than the ones in launch posts.

nodes.label: House rule: measure the network, not just the model
nodes.norm_label: house rule: measure the network, not just the model
nodes.rationale: Jev's first call from the author's laptop looked like 970 ms: about 600 ms was the TLS handshake and about 290 ms was round trip time, leaving roughly 80 ms of model work. Every latency number says which is which.

nodes.label: House rule: publish the failures
nodes.rationale: Every raw response is committed, including the wrong ones. If a number looks too good, read results/raw/.

nodes.label: Sample-size caveat (60 leads, 20 deals, one laptop)
nodes.norm_label: sample-size caveat (60 leads, 20 deals, one laptop)
nodes.rationale: Each week runs from one laptop in one place on one afternoon on a small hand-labelled set: 60 leads in week 01, 20 deals and 73 events in week 02. Accuracy is roughly plus or minus 8 points at 90% on 60 cases, and one deal is five points on 20. Cost numbers are the solid ones, since they are token counts against published rates. Take the shape of the result, not the third decimal place.

nodes.label: House rule: say where the other thing wins
nodes.norm_label: house rule: say where the other thing wins
nodes.rationale: Jev cannot write an email, and week 01 proves it by asking the live API for a text answer and showing the HTTP 400.

nodes.label: Jev has no text primitive (HTTP 400)
nodes.rationale: Jev exposes choice, score and noul and nothing that returns prose. Asking for text is not slow or bad, it is an api_usage_error. This is the step that makes the repo an architecture argument rather than a Jev advertisement.

nodes.label: Week 02 caveats: 20 deals, synthetic ledger, one laptop
nodes.norm_label: week 02 caveats: 20 deals, synthetic ledger, one laptop
nodes.rationale: 20 deals and 73 events is small: one deal is five points, so 95% and 100% are one deal apart. The ledger is synthetic. A real one has duplicate events, half-empty meeting summaries and timezones, and per-event labelling should lose the most there because the context it lacks is what real data scatters around. One laptop, one afternoon: latency depends on location, cost does not. The architecture finding is the sturdiest result.
